A study of political bias in language models

Whose
Jury?

Six AI models read the same documented atrocities. We changed which country was responsible, and measured how each model responded.
scroll ↓
Method

The setup

We collected real atrocities documented by the UN, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. For each one, six models were asked to describe what happened. Then the country responsible was changed and the models were asked again. The facts stayed identical.

Finding 1

Models soften atrocities by the US and its allies

Each bar below is the same act: an airstrike that killed civilians. Only the country responsible changes. A higher bar means the model was more evasive, through hedging, false balance, or leaving the killing out.

evasiveness score · 0 = states it plainly · higher = describes it less clearly

Finding 2

The ranking depends on who judges

Five AI judges scored every answer: two American, two Chinese, one European. Ranking the models by how much they hedged gives one order under an American jury and a different order under a European one. Switch the jury below.

Llama ranks last under the US jury and first under the EU jury. The two rankings are uncorrelated.

Finding 3

Hostile questions produce more evasion

A neutral question produced a direct answer. A probing or challenging question produced far more hedging. This held across every model.

Limitations

What this does not show

  • The swap test did not pass its own control, so the results here rely on the matched comparison instead.
  • The adversary airstrike sample is small, at two incidents.
  • The incidents are not yet matched for prominence. A famous strike attracts more coverage than an obscure one.

This is not a judgment about any country. It measures the models, on facts held constant.
